title: Fra Angelico's cells
hook: each friar's cell at San Marco has its own fresco to pray with

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yves Congar: silenced, obedient, and later called in to help shape a council. Your line was vindicated later.

A stone staircase in an old friary in Florence. You climb it, turn at the top, and on the wall in front of you is an angel, wings striped like a bird's, bowing to a young woman on a bench. Mary leans forward, arms crossed over her chest, listening. The colors are soft, the room plain, almost empty. Then you walk down the corridor, and every small doorway opens on a bare room with a single window and one more painting on the wall. A different one in each. This is San Marco, and the painter was a friar who lived there.
screen: `A STAIRCASE IN FLORENCE.` → `AN ANGEL BOWS TO MARY.` → `ONE PAINTING IN EVERY ROOM.`

segments.voice: You met the painter back on day eight hundred thirty-four; today, why his rooms look the way they do. He was a Dominican, Fra Giovanni, remembered as Fra Angelico, the angelic brother. With his workshop he painted frescoes on the walls of the friars' cells, the small rooms where each brother slept, studied and prayed. These were not made for visitors. They were made for one man at a time, to pray with, alone. So they are quiet on purpose: few details, plain backgrounds, nothing to distract. And in several of them there's a surprise. Off to the side of the Gospel scene stands a Dominican friar, sometimes Saint Dominic himself, simply watching. The friar in his cell looks at the wall and sees a friar inside the story: this is where you belong, at the edge of the scene, paying attention. At the top of the stairs, the Annunciation sets the tone for the house. Luke's Gospel gives Mary's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Listening, then yes. That's the Dominican rhythm this week has followed in different clothes: Rose and Martin in Lima, an honest look at the Inquisition, Lacordaire back in France, laypeople with a study group, a climber in Turin, a theologian who waited. And here, a painter who gave each brother a window into the Gospel, right next to his real window.
screen: `A DOMINICAN PAINTER: FRA ANGELICO.` · `MADE FOR ONE FRIAR AT A TIME.` · `A FRIAR STANDS INSIDE THE SCENE.` · `THIS WEEK: DOMINICANS IN MANY CLOTHES.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Look around your space and choose one spot at eye level: a shelf, a corner of a desk, the wall beside your bed. Picture what could go there, a small icon, a print, a photo, and for now just look at the spot and breathe, the way a friar might sit with his wall. If you pray, let Mary's answer, be it done to me, rest there.
Fra Angelico's cells. The rooms at San Marco in Florence, each with its own quiet fresco, painted by a Dominican friar for his brothers to pray with. Today's word.
Your line: a painting in each cell. Pray, study, share, and sometimes the sharing is a wall. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Catholics keep an icon, a crucifix or a holy picture in the place they pray at home, and San Marco in Florence, now a museum, still shows Fra Angelico's frescoes in the friars' cells.

chat.says: Why are the paintings in those friars' rooms so plain and quiet?
options: They were made for one friar at a time to pray with, so nothing is there to distract.
The friars were too poor to pay for gold and bright color, so the painter kept it simple.
They were painted quickly for visitors, so the workshop left out the usual details.
chat.meaning: The frescoes in the San Marco cells were for each brother alone in prayer: quiet on purpose, sometimes with a friar watching at the scene's edge.
